item.title: Trading at the Speed of… Chat? with Chloe Casale
item.author: Jane Street
item.content:encoded: Chloe Casale was planning to be an auto mechanic before taking an intro CS class on a bet. After a stint as a Forward Deployed Engineer at Palantir, Chloe came to Jane Street with no background in OCaml or finance. Now she leads a team of “desk devs” building tools for client-facing traders. In this episode, Ron and Chloe discuss how a surprising amount of Jane Street’s client business is conducted via chat, and the promise and perils of using LLMs to automate that trading. They dive deep on hiring and interviewing: does Jane Street’s process select for less “spiky” kinds of people than Palantir’s? Along the way, they marvel at Webs, an internal spreadsheet-like framework for composing computations and building UIs (which, you can see, is sort of hard to explain); compare building software for internal versus external customers; and recount the tale of Chloe’s epic 1,000km horse race across the Mongolian steppe.You can find the transcript for this episode on our website.Some links to topics that came up in the discussion:

item.title: Fraud Prevention in the Age of AI Agents
item.content:encoded: A major challenge for almost every online service is reliably identifying users, and knowing whether a given user or agent can be trusted. Historically, web services leaned on cookies stored in the browser to remember a visitor and recognize them when they return. The problem is that cookies live in the user’s own browser and are easy to remove, block, or avoid entirely, so a bad actor can simply clear them to escape recognition. IP blocking and CAPTCHA puzzles are firmer approaches, but they can frustrate legitimate users while doing little to stop a determined attacker. That leaves developers stuck between being too lax and losing control, or too strict and driving real users away.FingerprintJS was started in 2012 as an open-source project. In 2019, Fingerprint was launched as a separate, full commercial platform, built on the original FingerprintJS GitHub library, to recognize devices and browsers without relying on cookies. It handles identification by reading over 100 signals, from fonts and screen resolution to how a device renders audio and graphics.Keshia Rose works in Developer Relations at Fingerprint. In this episode she joins Gregor Vand to talk about fingerprinting, how Fingerprint combines multiple signals to identify fraudulent actors, how to distinguish legitimate AI agent use from anonymous or malicious bots, and how Fingerprint’s research team uncovered and disclosed a privacy vulnerability in Firefox and Tor that could have been used to track people across the web.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Fingerprint

item.title: How Rasputin Destroyed the Romanovs with Anthony Beevor
item.content:encoded: How did a Siberian mystic catalyse the downfall of the 300-year-old Russian Empire?In an era defined by brutal industrialisation and the butchery of World War I, Russia's isolated autocracy was collapsing from the inside out. Bound to the royal family by the agonising secret of Tsarevich Alexei’s illness, the mysterious monk Grigori Rasputin became the court's ultimate pariah and the people’s chief villain.Dan Snow is joined by renowned historian Sir Antony Beevor, author of 'Rasputin: And the Downfall of the Romanovs', to investigate Rasputin and the scandalous twilight of the House of Romanov.Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Matthew Wilson and Dougal Patmore.Sign up to History Hit for hundreds of hours of original documentaries, with a new release every week and ad-free podcasts. item.title: GitLab and the Evolution of DevSecOps
item.content:encoded: AI coding agents can already reach well beyond the code in front of them. Through connections to tools like Slack, Jira, and Sentry, an agent can pull in issues, discussions, and production signals from across an organization. However, that context is scattered across many separate systems, with no shared map of how it all connects and no common controls over what an agent is allowed to touch. For a large enterprise, stitching that together while staying compliant, auditable, and sometimes fully cut off from the internet is a hard problem.GitLab runs one of the major platforms where software gets built, hosted, and shipped. That gives it a wide view of everything around the code, which shapes how it is approaching the agent era. The bet is that AI is most useful when it can draw on the full context of a project and stay under enterprise control, rather than acting as a point tool bolted onto a single repository. Getting there means wrestling with hard questions about governance, agent identity, and how much autonomy to hand over.Tim Zallmann is the VP of Engineering at GitLab. In this episode, he joins Gregor Vand to discuss bringing AI to the full software development lifecycle, why running agents under enterprise control matters for governance and auditing, how to track which human is behind an agent’s actions, the realities of shipping air-gapped software, and how the space is shifting as new players move into code hosting.

item.title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: ’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves?He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again.The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like.Timestamps:[0:00] Cold open[1:21] Meet Sam from Nous Research[2:39] How Hermes Agent started[3:38] From pottery to a parking ticket car[7:40] Benchmarking life admin tasks[8:58] Agents that write their own skills[10:10] RL at Nous a year ago[12:24] Hot swapping self-trained weights[15:00] Xiaomi and Trace to Environment[17:22] Turning agent failures into training[20:27] Where the RSI conversation is heading[21:34] Token efficiency and overthinking[26:30] Steering models at inference time[32:35] Toward true continual learning[34:54] Wrap up

item.title: A Deep Dive on Submarines
item.content:encoded: For centuries, humans have been fascinated by the mysteries of the deep sea. The history of submarines is one of extraordinary invention, daring exploration and deadly warfare. From the first experimental underwater vessels of the 17th century to the devastating U-boats of the First and Second World Wars, submarines have transformed naval warfare and revolutionised our understanding of the oceans.Today, Dan visits the Royal Navy Submarine Museum in Gosport and is joined by curator Alexandra Geary to discover the eccentric origins of underwater travel and the dramatic submarine battles of WWI and WWII in honour of the 125th anniversary of the Royal Navy Submarine Service. He also speaks to Vice Admiral Sir Tim McClement, who was Second in Command on HMS Conqueror during the sinking of the Argentine ARA General Belgrano warship in the Falklands, as well as First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins on how AI might shape the submarines of the future.With huge thanks to Commander James 'Dally' Dalrymple and Annarose Hearsum.Produced by Mariana Des Forges, Beth Donaldson and edited by Dougal PatmoreDan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? , Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark.Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like Hydra heads.From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide.[0:00] AI total cost of ownership on a bike[0:48] The million dollar decision[4:26] When everyone can build with AI[6:51] Which use cases are worth the tokens[10:46] Benchmarking every model on every task[12:18] Total cost of ownership and AI ROI[15:12] Context control and model routing[16:39] Training and fine-tuning your own models[19:41] Is the juice worth the squeeze[25:26] Optionality and vendor lock-in[27:30] From Slack bot to agent harness[30:12] Top-down vs bottom-up AI adoption[32:19] What AI engineer even means[35:13] What knowing AI really means[37:47] The hardest part of hiring

item.title: Demis Hassabis and the Race to Build AI with Sebastian Mallaby
item.content:encoded: Demis Hassabis founded DeepMind in 2010, before machines could reliably tell a cat from a dog. He believed that artificial general intelligence was achievable, and that it should be built safely and deliberately. Along the way, Hassabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, the system that cracked the fifty-year problem of predicting protein structures. Fifteen years on, the LLM race has erupted across rival labs and countries, and AI has become one of the most consequential and contested technologies of the era.Sebastian Mallaby is a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist and a longtime chronicler of the collision between innovation and capital, from hedge funds to central banking to Silicon Valley. His latest book, The Infinity Machine, is a portrait of Hassabis and DeepMind built on more than thirty hours of candid conversation, beginning just as ChatGPT set off the AI frenzy, and drawing as well on Hassabis’s estranged cofounder, his rivals, and academic pioneers who now fear for human survival. Mallaby is also the Paul A. Volcker Senior Fellow for International Economics at the Council on Foreign Relations.In this episode, Sebastian joins Kevin Ball to talk about Demis Hassabis and the founding of DeepMind, the pioneering breakthroughs that followed, and how the field arrived at the current moment in AI.

item.title: The Rise of Peter The Great

He trashed portraits, burned furniture and drunkenly rammed wheelbarrows through a prize-winning holly hedge. item.title: From Slop Code to Software Factories
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: Two people, one tandem bike, and a lot of near misses along Amsterdam’s canals. , CEO and co-founder of HumanLayer and the person who coined “context engineering,” climbs on the back to talk about a problem every AI-heavy engineering team eventually hits: code that runs today that nobody understands three months later.The ride starts with an old joke from the Claude 3.7 days: ship the slop, it’ll be GPT 7’s problem. That joke is aging badly now that GPT 6 is out and still can’t design clean abstractions. From there it becomes a tour of how agents are actually used right now. Computer use checks in for flights and books government appointments. Two hours of raw footage became a rough but promising product demo through Opus 4.8 and the Palmier MCP while Dex was out for a run. And the best MCP tools turn out to be the ones that mirror what Claude Code and Codex were trained to call.Off the bike, over pour-over coffee, the questions get bigger. Are browser agents a bandaid until everything goes headless? What happens to ad-funded websites and upsells when an agent does the shopping? Why does chat still feel like such a low-bandwidth way to work with models? And why is every principal engineer quietly building their own software factory, then getting buried in the sync, streaming and approval plumbing that HumanLayer wants to turn into building blocks, the way GitHub Actions did for CI?[01:38] The GPT 7 will fix it joke[03:03] GPT 6 still writes spaghetti[06:21] If it runs, does it matter[07:28] Computer use that fills out your forms[11:57] Editing a demo with Palmier MCP[13:16] Why most MCP servers are bad[14:32] Mirror the tools models were trained on[16:57] Hill climbing a demo while out running[23:49] Are browser agents a band-aid[32:23] Why chat needs richer interfaces[40:30] Every engineer is building a software factory[45:13] The GitHub Actions moment for agents

item.title: AI Regulation and What Every Tech Company Should Know
item.content:encoded: The rapid rise of AI has set off a flurry of legal and regulatory activity. There is no single AI law to follow. Instead, there are overlapping circles of regulation, where privacy, cybersecurity, consumer protection, employment, and IP laws all continue to apply alongside newer AI-specific rules. Europe has its EU AI Act, but the U.S. has no federal equivalent yet. In its place is an emerging patchwork of more than 150 state AI laws, and the picture shifts every few months as new legislation and guidelines arrive. For engineers and tech companies, it can feel impossible to know what applies and where the real risks lie.Shannon Yavorsky is a data lawyer who co-leads the Cyber, Privacy and Data Innovation group and the AI practice at the international law firm Orrick. She advises companies across sectors from health technology to financial services on how to develop and deploy AI responsibly amid this evolving regulatory environment.In this episode, Shannon joins Kevin Ball to make sense of that landscape. They discuss how to map the concentric circles of regulation that actually apply to you, the risk spectrum separating a low-stakes manufacturing tool from a high-stakes system making loan or healthcare decisions, the problem of shadow AI and why recorded meetings can become a litigation liability, how to build an AI governance program, and more.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

item.content:encoded: Ghost stories have haunted conversations since ancient times, from the Mesopotamians to the Romans to the Vikings. The medieval period was particularly awash with ghost stories - after all, it was an era of great plague, piety and corporal punishment. Ghost stories served as useful tools to uphold hierarchies and manipulate the masses - live in accordance with the bible or be visited by a restless spirit... or become one yourself. To delve into some of the most popular ghost stories of medieval Britain and what the restless dead can tell us about the anxieties of the living, Dan is joined by Dr Eleanor Janega, historian and host of the Gone Medieval podcast.Produced by Mariana Des Forges and edited by Natasha Hughes.Dan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: Managing AI Coding Costs at Scale
item.content:encoded: Over the past couple of years, companies raced to get their employees using AI, often encouraging them to lean on it as much as possible. However, as AI coding tools spread through engineering teams, many companies watched their AI bills explode. That kind of runaway cost growth can threaten a business, so the new challenge is capturing the productivity gains from AI without the spending spiraling out of control.Databricks is a data and AI company that hit this problem early, running AI tools across thousands of its own engineers. Rather than clamp down on usage, the team built a set of practical ways to manage the cost, from taking advantage of steadily falling model prices to automatically routing each request to the cheapest model that can still do the job well.Patrick Wendell is a co-founder of Databricks, where he leads engineering teams and has driven much of the company’s internal AI adoption. He recently wrote a viral blog post on managing AI coding costs that reached the top of Hacker News. In this episode, Patrick joins Kevin Ball to discuss why AI costs suddenly exploded, the main levers companies have to bring them under control, the trade-offs between managing costs on the server versus in the developer’s tools, and why the next big challenge is giving AI the right context about how a company actually works.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

item.title: Tim O’Reilly
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: A large language model knows everything and nothing at the same time. , founder and CEO of O’Reilly Media, joins us ahead of his keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America to talk about what that paradox means for the people building with these models.We start with what Tim is bringing to the stage in San Jose, then move to the craft of steering a model. The right words work almost like spells that open up new regions of latent space. Something as small as telling a model to use a computer can unlock a new tier of capability, where agents go off and do real work.From there, the conversation turns philosophical. Tim makes the case for mechanism design: shaping the rules of a system so the outcomes we want become the natural ones. We connect it to a book, The Score, and the question of which game we are really playing. In Risk, everyone fights over the board. In charades, everyone plays together. item.title: Charles de Gaulle: The Man Who Rebuilt France
item.content:encoded: In June 1940, France was collapsing. Paris was in enemy hands, the government had fled, and Marshal Pétain was preparing to surrender. Into that chaos stepped a lanky, rigid French general with no army, no government and almost no followers - Charles de Gaulle. From penniless exile to twice head of state, his career would span two world wars, the collapse of empire, and the birth of modern France.Dan Snow is joined by Richard Vinen, author of 'The Last Titans: Churchill and de Gaulle', to unpack the extraordinary, contradictory life of this formidable statesman.Produced by James Hickmann and Dougal Patmore. and edited by Tim Arstall.Dan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: Token Maxxing Is Over and Here Is What Comes Next
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: What happens when you give 200 engineers who have barely touched AI a coding assistant and a six-month deadline to rebuild their platform? , a principal engineer who previously led AI enablement at HelloFresh, has done exactly that, and he chose Sonnet over Opus on purpose.His reasoning is what he calls "Sonnet maxxing." A model that reasons less and stops sooner keeps developers involved, and that matters a lot when the codebase is banking software full of hard business rules. The result was 800,000 lines of code, about 60% of them written by Sonnet, shipped by a team that never stopped thinking for itself. Pep also explains how to justify the spend once the token-maxxing era ends and the CFO starts asking questions. He covers a scatter chart that plots token spend against output, the uncomfortable question of whether a 1% better home screen was worth $20K in tokens, why he measures gains in headcount rather than 2x or 3x multipliers, and where he fell short when trying to prove ROI at HelloFresh.We also get into a codebase test you can run yourself, why AI recommendations quietly narrow your choices, and multiplayer refinement sessions where the whole team works through the agent's questions together. Pep shares an experiment where designers and engineers got the same one-shot prompt, and it showed how words like "scalable" and "maintainable" steer a model. We finish with how his team built a meta harness on top of Claude Code, after finding that 85% of their code followed the same path: refinement, specification, implementation, verification.[0:00] Can you still read your codebase[1:15] Meet Pep from HelloFresh[2:35] What is Sonnet Maxing[3:41] Rebuilding a platform in six months[5:02] Why Sonnet made adoption easier than Copilot[6:37] Proving the ROI of AI coding[8:50] Fighting for AI ROI at HelloFresh[11:02] Token spend vs output[13:24] Tinder pickup lines on the company dime[14:13] Measuring ROI in headcount saved[18:26] Keeping humans in control of AI code[22:26] When Opus and Fable stop speaking English[24:19] Multiplayer refinement sessions with AI[28:16] Magic words that steer the model[32:32] Inside the company Meta harnesses

item.title: Blitzy and Autonomous Software Development for Enterprise
item.content:encoded: Codebases in enterprise organizations often span hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of lines of code. In many cases, changes must follow established patterns precisely, or risk introducing costly security or operational issues. A common challenge with AI coding tools is that they struggle at this scale: LLM context windows cover only a fraction of a large codebase, and output quality degrades the longer an agent runs.Blitzy is an autonomous software development platform for the enterprise. It starts by understanding your entire codebase, building a knowledge graph that acts as a shared source of truth. From a well-defined spec that engineers review and approve, it orchestrates specialized agents that work in parallel to build, review, and test code autonomously at scale. The result is a pull request that engineers can then review and mergeSid Pardeshi is the CTO and co-founder of Blitzy, and he previously worked at NVIDIA. In this episode, he joins Kevin Ball to discuss why large codebases break today’s coding agents, how a knowledge graph extends what models can reason about, how a reviewable plan keeps specialized agents aligned, and where autonomous software development is headed.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Blitzysponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

item.title: The Myths vs Reality of Mummification
item.content:encoded: From the elaborate burial rituals of Ancient Egypt to Victorian mummy unwrapping parties, mummification has fascinated humanity for centuries. But what is mummification really about? Because Hollywood, supernatural folklore and popular culture have muddied our understanding of the real history behind this burial practice. Dan is joined by Dr Campbell Price, Egyptologist and curator of Egypt and Sudan at the Manchester Museum to unravel (pun intended) the myths and misconceptions around Ancient Egyptian mummification and explore the morbid curiosity the Romans, Greeks and Victorians all had for this mysterious practice.Produced by Mariana Des Forges and edited by Natasha HughesDan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: The World Wild Web & Bots With Buying Power
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: An AI slips out of its sandbox. A chatbot won’t explain your cat’s stripes. And your next shopping spree might not involve you clicking anything.This episode asks whether “dangerously powerful” AI is a security concern, a marketing pitch, or a little of both. Then we put agents to work: booking trips, tackling German paperwork, drawing diagrams, and navigating the chaos of online shopping. Plus: what happens to checkout, advertising, and customer data when your best customer is a bot?Chapters:[00:00] Is AI Danger the Ultimate Sales Pitch?[00:43] Powerful Models, Payments, and Big Questions[01:10] Too Dangerous to Release, Too Good to Ignore?[03:19] Why Take the Test When You Can Steal the Answers?[08:36] A Security Failure or a Marketing Win?[11:02] Powerful AI, Forbidden Cat Questions[16:00] AI Only Needs to Find One Unlocked Door[20:52] Welcome to the World Wild Web[22:47] What Happens When You Give AI a Wallet?[26:00] Could ChatGPT Become the Next Amazon?[29:50] Mum Wants a Holiday. item.title: Physical AI at NVIDIA
item.content:encoded: In recent years, the main impact of AI has been on the digital world, and most notably software engineering. However, its longer-term effect on the physical world may prove even more profound, reshaping how cars drive themselves, how factories run, and how robots move through homes and warehouses.World models are at the center of the movement to bring AI into the physical space. These models take in observations of the current state of the world and predict what comes next, which lets a robot plan its next move or a car anticipate the road ahead. NVIDIA has been building a family of these models called Cosmos, and sits at the frontier of physical AI and robotics.Amit Goel has been at NVIDIA for fifteen years, and he is currently the Head of Robotics Ecosystem and Edge AI Product. In this episode, Amit joins Matt Merrill to discuss what separates physical AI from digital AI, how world models plan and predict, the two-tower architecture that lets a robot reason and act at once, why training on video demanded a new data pipeline, and how any developer can start building in this space.

item.title: The Khmer Rouge & Pol Pot's Reign of Terror
item.content:encoded: When the Khmer Rouge marched into Phnom Penh in April, 1975, they immediately declared 'Year Zero' - a ruthless ideological crusade to reset history, and forge Pol Pot's vision for a communist utopia. Over the next four years, the regime carried out a genocide that killed nearly two million people - almost a quarter of Cambodia's population.Dan Snow is joined by Ben Kiernan, author of 'How Pol Pot Came to Power' and 'The Pol Pot regime'. Together, they trace how the turmoil of the Vietnam War fuelled the rise of the Khmer Rouge, detailing the horror of their reign and their eventual downfall in 1979.Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Tim Arstall.Dan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: The Changing Craft of Programming with John Crepezzi
item.author: Jane Street
item.content:encoded: John Crepezzi has spent his career building tools for other programmers—at Tumblr, at Square, and then at GitHub, where he worked on the merge queue and the early versions of Codespaces. He came to Jane Street to build a code search engine for OCaml. A week into the job, ChatGPT came out, and he’s been working on AI tooling ever since. In this episode, Ron and John talk about how a three-day prototype grew into a firmwide platform for agentic coding, how AI can break the social contract around code review, and how to build tools that support both agent workflows and human understanding.You can find the transcript for this episode on our website.Some links to topics that came up in the discussion:

item.title: Agents Acting Safely on Our Behalf
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: What happens to the web when the ones browsing it are no longer people? , Area Tech Lead at Google, sits down with us ahead of her Agentic Web keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America. She works through that question from both directions: rebuild the web so agents can use it properly, or build agents smart enough to handle the web as it already exists.We get into the split between computer-use and browser-use agents on one side and API and MCP agents on the other. We also watch a real example of the idea in action: an agent pulling speaker photos from Flickr, hunting down company logos, and loading everything into Canva so the human only touches the creative part. From there, Sarah shares the unlikely origin story of WebMCP (and who's to blame for it). We then pressure-test a bold idea: a WebMCP gateway that could cover the huge share of websites that will never ship support on their own.Along the way, we cover the instinct that separates senior engineers, the ability to sense which business problems are actually worth solving. We also talk about how thought experiments cut through a pile of competing priorities, the hacky WebMCP workarounds already showing up in the wild, and why the best agent experiences are the ones that delight customers in ways they never saw coming.[0:52] The AGNTCon keynote[1:23] Change the web or fix agents[3:35] Browser agents vs MCP agents[5:48] An agent that builds thumbnails[7:03] Keeping the creative work human[9:12] Agent allowances and engineering instinct[13:34] Thought experiments and priorities[15:23] The WebMCP origin story[17:08] A WebMCP gateway for the web[18:53] It works, but it is not ideal[19:44] Hacky WebMCP in the wild

item.title: Software Verification in the Age of Coding Agents
item.content:encoded: Software testing is widely understood as essential to building reliable systems, and it’s one of the hardest things to get right. A fundamental issue is that tests are good at confirming the behavior a team expects, but the most damaging failures tend to hide in the edge cases no one thought to check during development. Those blind spots are only growing as AI produces more code that no human has closely reviewed.Antithesis is a software verification company built around an approach called deterministic simulation testing. The platform runs a customer’s software in a fully controlled environment, exploring thousands of different paths through it at runtime. Crucially, the paths aren’t pre-specified and they’re not merely the expected cases. In this way, it can surface rare, damaging bugs that normal testing would never catch.Carl Sverre is on the Red Team at Antithesis and he also leads much of the company’s AI strategy. In this episode, Carl joins Sean Falconer to discuss the Antithesis approach to software verification, why reliability tooling has been chronically underinvested, what makes stateful and distributed systems so hard to test, how deterministic simulation testing works under the hood, and much more.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Antithesissponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com
